prompt.context: Your client is a large pharmaceutical drug company working on a vaccine for chicken pox. The vaccine needs to pass three phases of testing to be approved by the FDA. It has just completed the second phase and the client is asking your help to decide if they should fund the third phase. The third phase would last 2 years, cost $300M, and results from previous phases indicate the vaccine has a 95% chance of approval. We would be able to start producing vaccine immediately following approval.
prompt.question: Should the client fund the third and final phase of testing for the chicken pox vaccine? Go or No-go?

clarifying_info.q: Which market are we focusing on?
clarifying_info.a: We are only worried about the US market in this case.

clarifying_info.q: What form does the vaccine take?
clarifying_info.a: The vaccine is a one-time pill.

clarifying_info.q: What is the US population and its age distribution?
clarifying_info.a: Assume US population is 300M, uniformly distributed from age 0 to 75 (as many people enter as leave every year).

clarifying_info.q: What portion of the population would need the vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: [Hand candidate Exhibit 1 — Cumulative Distribution of Chicken Pox Exposure]

clarifying_info.q: How long would it take to vaccinate the existing population?
clarifying_info.a: It is estimated that it would take 3 years to vaccinate the existing population.
[Hand candidate Exhibit 2 — Parent's Willingness to Pay and ask them to estimate the price]

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs per pill?
clarifying_info.a: Distribution $1.50, Production $2.50, SG&A $5.00 — total $9.00 per pill. The $300M phase-three cost covers everything else (plant setup, etc.) and can be spread over the 2 years of testing.
The vaccine will not be patented.

clarifying_info.q: Are other companies testing a similar vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: No other companies have started formal testing. Other companies would have to undergo the same series of testing. Phase 1 and 2 combined take 3 years, so we have approximately 3 years of competitive protection. Phase 1 and 2 cost $200M.

exhibits.title: Cumulative Distribution of Chicken Pox Exposure
exhibits.shows: A cumulative distribution curve showing the percentage of the population that has been exposed to chicken pox by a given age. The curve rises from 0% at birth, reaches roughly 50% around age 9, and approaches 100% by age 18-21.

data.key_points: ~50% exposed by age 9; ~100% exposed by age 18-21

exhibits.title: Parent's Willingness to Pay
exhibits.shows: A demand curve showing the percentage of parents willing to purchase the vaccine at various price points. The curve slopes downward from left to right as price increases.

data.y_axis: Percentage of parents willing to pay (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%)
data.key_points: ~100% willing at ~$10; 75% willing at ~$30; 50% willing at ~$35; 25% willing at ~$40

framework: Define the decision: NPV of funding Phase 3 vs. walking away (sunk costs of Phases 1 and 2 are irrelevant)
Estimate market size: segment into (a) existing unvaccinated population and (b) annual newborns
Estimate revenue: determine addressable units, willingness-to-pay, and optimal price point
Estimate costs: per-pill variable costs plus Phase 3 investment as fixed cost
Build a multi-year cash flow table and assess NPV directionally
Assess competitive landscape: barriers to entry, competitive response, sustainability of position
Synthesize: Go/No-go recommendation with key risks

questions.prompt: Part 1 — Market sizing: How many people need the vaccine and when?
questions.guidance: Candidate should split the market into two segments. Segment A (existing population): US population 300M, uniform 0-75, so 4M people per age year. Exhibit 1 shows ~50% exposed by age 9 and ~100% by age 18-21, implying roughly half of the 0-18 cohort has NOT been exposed (i.e., needs the vaccine). That gives 4M * 18 * 0.5 = 36M unvaccinated people in the existing population. At 75% WTP (from Exhibit 2 at $30): 36M * 0.75 = 27M paying customers, vaccinated over 3 years = 9M/year. Segment B (new babies): 4M born per year (steady-state), 75% of parents willing to pay = 3M/year ongoing. A strong answer identifies both segments and notes the time horizon differences.

math.setup: Segment A (existing unvaccinated): 300M pop / 75 ages = 4M per age cohort. Ages 0-18 unexposed = 4M * 18 * 50% = 36M. At 75% WTP = 27M over 3 years = 9M/year. Segment B (new babies): 4M/year * 75% = 3M/year.
steps: 36M * 75% WTP = 27M paying customers from existing population
27M / 3 years = 9M vaccines per year for years 1-3 post-approval
4M births/year * 75% WTP = 3M new baby vaccines per year (ongoing)
math.answer: 9M vaccines/year for first 3 years post-approval (existing pop) + 3M vaccines/year thereafter (new babies)

questions.prompt: Part 1 — Pricing: What price should the client set?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 2 to identify the profit-maximizing price. At $30 the willingness-to-pay is 75% — consistent with the 75% figure used in market sizing above. Variable cost per pill = $1.50 + $2.50 + $5.00 = $9.00. Contribution margin at $30 = $21/pill. Candidate should confirm $30 is optimal and tie the price chosen back to the same 75% WTP rate used in the market sizing.

math.answer: $21 contribution margin per pill at $30 price

questions.prompt: Part 1 — Cash flow and NPV: Build the revenue and cost schedule and assess whether NPV is positive.
questions.guidance: Candidate should construct a year-by-year table. Years 1-2 are Phase 3 testing — cash outflow of $150M/year, no revenue. Approval at end of year 2, commercial launch year 3. Years 3-5: 12M vaccines/year (9M existing + 3M babies) * $21 margin = $252M net/year. From year 6 onward: 3M vaccines/year * $21 = $63M/year. Candidate does not need to calculate exact NPV — they should recognize it is highly positive given large positive cash flows beginning year 3. Candidate should also note the 5% failure risk (correct treatments: multiply expected cash flows by 0.95, or note the 5% downside scenario is losing $300M which is small relative to the upside).

math.setup: Year-by-year net cash flow table in $M. Phase 3 investment in Years 1-2; commercial launch Year 3. Units in millions of vaccines; revenue and costs in $M.
steps: Year 1: Existing pop vaccines = 0, New baby vaccines = 0, Total = 0, Revenue = 0, Costs = -150 (Phase 3), Net = -150
Year 2: Existing pop vaccines = 0, New baby vaccines = 0, Total = 0, Revenue = 0, Costs = -150 (Phase 3), Net = -150
Year 3: Existing pop = 9M, New babies = 3M, Total = 12M, Revenue = 12*30 = 360, Costs = 12*9 = 108, Net = 252
Year 4: Existing pop = 9M, New babies = 3M, Total = 12M, Revenue = 360, Costs = 108, Net = 252
Year 5: Existing pop = 9M, New babies = 3M, Total = 12M, Revenue = 360, Costs = 108, Net = 252
Year 6+: Existing pop = 0, New babies = 3M, Total = 3M, Revenue = 3*30 = 90, Costs = 3*9 = 27, Net = 63 per year
NPV qualitative: $252M * 3 years = $756M gross in years 3-5 alone, far outweighs $300M investment even at a high pharma discount rate, plus perpetuity of $63M/year.
math.answer: Net: -$150M, -$150M, +$252M, +$252M, +$252M, +$63M/year thereafter. NPV is strongly positive at any reasonable pharma discount rate.

questions.prompt: Part 2 — Competitive landscape: Will competitors enter and threaten our position?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize: (1) The vaccine is not patented, so competitors could legally enter. (2) However, competitors must go through the same Phase 1 + 2 testing (3 years, $200M) before starting Phase 3. This gives our client ~3 years of first-mover exclusivity on the existing unvaccinated population. (3) By the time competitors could enter (year 6 from now / year 3 post-launch), the entire existing unvaccinated population has already been vaccinated. Competitors would only compete for the 3M new babies/year market. (4) Competitors would need to spend $200M (Ph1+2) + $300M (Ph3) = $500M total to compete for a market generating only $63M/year — not economically attractive. Note: Phase 1+2 costs are sunk for our client but represent a real future cost for competitors, making our competitive position even stronger.

math.setup: Competitor economics if they entered at year 6
steps: Competitor addressable market = 3M babies/year (if they match $30 price and 75% WTP)
Even if competitor captures 50% of baby market: 1.5M * $21 margin = $31.5M/year
Payback period at $31.5M/year is over 15 years — unattractive at pharma hurdle rates
math.answer: Competitors have little economic incentive to enter; our first-mover advantage on the existing population is unchallenged.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors or risks should the client consider before making a final go/no-go decision?

categories.name: Market and demand risks
ideas: Natural herd immunity reduces addressable population over time
Vaccine hesitancy could lower actual WTP below exhibit estimates
Parents may not see value since chicken pox is generally mild
Changes in CDC or ACIP vaccination schedule recommendations

categories.name: Regulatory and Phase 3 risks
ideas: 5% chance Phase 3 fails FDA approval — entire $300M investment lost
FDA could require additional post-approval studies
Label restrictions could limit the indicated population

categories.name: Competitive risks
ideas: A competitor may already be in advanced private testing not publicly known
A larger competitor could absorb testing costs as a strategic move
Licensing deal or partnership could lower competitor entry barriers

categories.name: Financial and strategic risks
ideas: Opportunity cost: $300M could be deployed on higher-NPV projects
Cost overruns in Phase 3 beyond the $300M budget
Portfolio fit: does chicken pox vaccine align with company therapeutic focus?

categories.name: Operational risks
ideas: Manufacturing scale-up risk: can the $300M budget cover plant setup adequately?
Distribution network capacity for rapid 3-year rollout to existing population
Pricing pressure from government payers or insurance companies

recommendation: Recommend GO — fund the third phase of testing for the chicken pox vaccine
NPV analysis shows strongly positive returns: approximately $756M in net cash flow in years 3-5 alone against a $300M investment, plus a perpetuity of $63M/year from the ongoing baby cohort
Competitive analysis confirms a natural 3-year first-mover advantage on the existing unvaccinated population; competitors have no economic incentive to enter the smaller residual market
risks: 5% probability of Phase 3 failure resulting in loss of the $300M investment
Actual vaccine uptake may be lower than the 75% WTP shown in Exhibit 2
Absence of patent protection leaves the residual baby market theoretically open to future competition
next_steps: Initiate Phase 3 trial immediately to maximize the competitive protection window
Finalize manufacturing and distribution partnerships so production can begin immediately upon FDA approval
Develop pricing and market access strategy including engagement with insurance payers and government formularies
Monitor competitor R&D pipelines for any signs of parallel development programs
